content.title: At the Threshold
content.subtitle: A short drama in one room
content.raw_content:
SCENE I: THE WRITING ROOM — DUSK

(A tall arched window reveals rain falling softly against old brick. A desk of dark cedar holds an inkwell and loose parchment.)

MARA
(Standing by the window, without turning)
You always leave the door ajar. As if a sentence might escape.

KAI
(Seated at the desk, dipping a nib into dark ink)
Sentences do escape, Mara. Especially the ones we never meant to say aloud.

MARA
(Turning slowly)
And what will you do when this one finds its reader?

KAI
Listen for the echo.

content.title: The First Garden
content.subtitle: An audio story on remembrance and quiet faith
content.raw_content:
In the first garden, nothing asked to be explained. Every green shoot, every damp petal in the morning sun, simply existed under the light.

We forget that waiting is also an act of faith. When the seasons turn sharp, we look for words that can steady us. This reading was recorded in the quiet hours of dusk, reflecting on where roots take hold when the ground feels unfamiliar.

content.title: On Stories That Refuse to Stay Quiet
content.subtitle: An introductory essay on voice, faith, and shared humanity
content.raw_content:
There is a particular kind of silence that precedes an honest sentence. It is not the silence of having nothing to say, but rather the quiet courage of deciding to say what has waited in the dark for too long.

I have learned that when we write from our deepest observations—from our faith, our quiet ache, our sudden joys—we rarely write alone. Between my private memory and your living heart, emotions meet. The circumstance of the story belongs to one person, but the feeling belongs to everyone who has ever walked through the door of another morning.

That is why this house exists. House of Wild Ink is built for the sentences that refuse to stay quiet in drawers, for the poems that demand to be recited against the noise of the day, and for the reflections that remind us that though we are all different stones, we are shaped by the same quiet earth.

content.title: Still Here
content.raw_content:
The sun is shining brightly
A beautiful day it is going to be
The wind blowing ever so lovely
The sky ever so shimmering blue
Oh! Life is amazingly beautiful.
Only yesterday the sun was out of sight
The day was moody and muddy
The wind was strong, too strong to be lovely
The sky was black, yea blanket black
And I didn’t think life amazingly beautiful.
Life is such as I have experienced
On certain days I feel like I could live forever
On others more often I want to do God a favor
The dishonor of taking my own life
If I did though, the sunny days I would not see.
And though I’ve never really gotten used to the frightening moments
Never stopped believing sometimes that me out of the picture would be
Would be the ultimate solution
I’m always glad after the dark and rainy days
That I am here, still here and alive, living in the sunny days.
8/12/2019

And they said, “I could not take it anymore, I wanted to be out of the mess, I wanted to be out of this world."
I knew it could not follow me where I would go. And I knew the world would miss me even if brief.

Revenge at life itself at its best, hurting myself even more to hurt them too, going away permanently to make them miss me temporarily.
But I still feel I won, because I am no longer here”.

content.title: Misplaced Priorities
content.raw_content:
In the dead of the night
Her soul immortal strode where mere men would dare not run
Empty she felt
Then like correction from the gods, she lived an aspect of her life
In that place where mere men would not run
An aspect it was
He was there, she saw and he saw
He saw she that he had fooled and she saw he whom she loved and yet regretted the mere thought of it
A fool, she thought herself
Then he said it, he said the very worlds that to the ancient had been known and yet eloped the girl till she was victim again and again
A fit she had, yet pain true she felt
Here, he compared her to another
Said another was better than her and asked how she could not have known the truth and told her how a fool she had been
Speechless it made her in anger enveloping
She was angry and yet she was hurt too
She allowed this, she placed another above herself
She reduced herself to nothing to give him pleasure because of what?
An answer then and now she could not find ….
Knowing in her inmost being the end was not what she wanted
She continued in the thought to not lose a friend
Yet he was not even a friend to be lost
In her fury, rage, hurt and disappointment, she beat him and yet not wanting to kill him.
She did that fearing what she would do to herself if she didn’t find a way to make him feel what she felt
Revenge now or never
But in the end, she was hurt. Her heart broken, she had been lied to, disappointed, used and onlookers would have a laugh and say, ‘I told her’, how could she not have known?
The pain and hurt she could not handle
Her immortal-self left the land where mere men would not run to  the land where mere men lived and ruled
She had brought with her wisdom, priceless wisdom, to not place another above herself.
To not reduce herself to nothing for a person; for when a true friend she could not find in another, she should find one in herself.
Self-love it is…

content.title: Fear
content.raw_content:
When darkness falls, would I find myself alone?
Now what do I fear at all? Darkness or being alone?
In the dark I think I see things or rather I think they see me.
And I know not where to hide.
Close my eyes or keep them wide open.
I still feel I am at the mercy of those things
Now is it when I am alone that darkness frightens me?
Those endless scary thoughts gnaw at my brain.
Oh!  That I would believe and understand
That all that I fear is all in my head and is there only because,
I let it and I feed it too.
How come during the day at the same places I move about fearlessly with friends or alone.

We are mere men acting out our roles.

Every man thinks first of himself and what best serves him first.
It is only the god – man who did what could first best serve others.
So one would have to become a man-god to play so close.
With that still, there are still some flaws.

content.title: When the Scene Ends
content.raw_content:
Does a story end with a scene?
Tis’ possible, I think.
Yet a scene could just be the link between other parts of a story.
A scene could just be a picture amongst others like it.
A scene could be the end without a beginning, a beginning without an end or a beginning and end without the story.
A scene, how important is it?
The out-play of parts of the story of a life.
A life lived, being lived, or yet to be lived,
Existence, it is…had been, is being or will be …. is made up of scenes.
Life begins and ends at a scene…and yes, any other scene is as important as the other.
When our individual stories end at a scene, what shall it be like?
Each day is like the realization of a part of our lives, a scene being acted out and watched say by a group of heavenly hosts.

content.title: Quatrains
content.raw_content:
This afternoon I had a siesta
By my side was Senorita
Together we had a fiesta
Then we decided to go to Volta.
Juanita tricked them and she was called a trickster
A beautiful song she sang after, then called a songster
I knew who she was, always would be a jokester
So I pranked her too and she called me a prankster.
Two weeks after forty and counting, still unmarried, still a spinster
Met a fine gentleman a week earlier, oh he was a keynoter
I had no idea he was not who he seemed to be, he was sinister
In return for love, I gave him my money but he was a fraudster.
His tears sloped down his cheeks and it tasted like seawater
Like a pastor she spoke the words that would his life alter
Her words pierced, and the purpose was not his life to better
She made her purpose clear then he knew it was his slaughter.
Today is a new day, a new page is opened, and to begin is a new chapter
Yesterday, I made mistakes and frenemies too, it was a complete clutter
Today I move forward, learning from mistakes and growing my character
Yesterday, all that happened I cannot change but I remember it as a prompter.

content.title: My Greatest Fear
content.raw_content:
I am afraid it would happen and I would be a fool to not have listened
But even more that bystanders would look upon me a good example of a bad example of another life yet wasted.
One who was spoken to but would not heed one who was constrained but would not remain.
Still, I am afraid I cannot do all they say.
I cannot follow everywhere they lead.
I cannot bind myself with the chains of regret from their mistakes.
My innate man wants to be free, free to live and not exist.
Free to ply the road taken by both many and few.
Free to make mistakes and learn, break an arm and heal.
Free to make choices based on experiences heard or learned first -hand.
Free to break rules so l can rule.
My fear is, my fear is I cannot remain in the cage made for me; to protect me they say.
My fear is that you wouldn’t understand that though I have heard your stories.
I can’t fight my heart’s leading; my heart’s desire and my fate to write mine exclusively.
My greatest fear is I cannot promise you that in living my life, I will break no rules….yours or mine… do you understand?

content.title: A Mark of a Life Lived
content.raw_content:
I wrote a poem which saw not the day.
I composed a song creation never heard.
I wrote a story though lovely never was read.
A picture I sketched never admired.
Dreams dreamt and like fairytales never were fulfilled.
My heart bleeds as tears sting my eyes.
My soul is shaken with a void insuppressible.
My mind awakens in the deep of the night.
My spirit tries endlessly to find the light.
A voice in my head so true, accusatory, yet too honest,
Asks the question I dread, the mark of a life lived.
What have you done with your talents and gifts?
When I awaken so shaken with guilt and fear of making light my talents and gifts,
I resolve to do much better with my time, so my creator my being may not despise
But what happens then after a couple of days of tos and fros?
I fall back into the rhythm, the rhythm of lack.
That it seems I was not gifted with luck,
The luck to have such gifts to show creation.
I fall back into the deception of ungratefulness.
But when I go back to lie down, in the deep of the night and in that place,
In the place the soul meets the spirit and they do commune of things which are.

content.title: With Her
content.raw_content:
Life I perceived to be monochromatic
Until she came my way and it all seemed polychromatic
Colorful is the theme of life
But I only understood that when she became my wife
Yet now together we began to face a rife
I am yet to find the answer though as I search the reason for our woes
But love is a beautiful thing, though it can hurt as much as a bee sting
Just as the turbulent waves disturb the ocean’s calmness,
I in love would take everything with which it comes
Or else to be fair to myself and to her, I would rather say that I know not how to love.

Maybe, someday, a little while, it shall be, the old rendered
That we shall live amongst them.

belief in myself?

Who is it that still believes in me and throws my way one chance
after the other?

written me off?
Who is it that still believes in me as a person and accepts me
for who I am and willing to assist me be better?
Who is it that still believes in me to magnify my strengths and
quieten my flaws?
Who is it? Who is it? Who is it?
Am I the only one who asks these questions?

content.title: An Inch Closer to the End
content.raw_content:
Sometimes just like you, I wish the truth was not strictly the truth and that a lie so innocent could just be my truth—a little more room for wrong.
It eases my guilt of sin and shame, and I am comforted knowin' I can be remorseful and always ask forgiveness from God.
But the devil be playin' us.
The devil be playin' us by makin' us believe there is still room for a little more sin.
Gosh, I like this girl and I like this boy, or this situation is just too hard right now to do the right thing.
I know my faith does not condone this, that sin is sin no matter how I justify it.
But let me fall just this once.
I will be back to seek forgiveness and continue working out my righteousness and salvation on this narrow path that I need to take a sinful break from every once in a while. Just when it is needed and I can not help it.
NO, NO, NO, DON'T LISTEN TO THE VOICE OF DECEPTION!

I say, “Love and submit first because you love.”

content.title: Broken Hearts
content.raw_content:
Broken hearts all around,Broken dreams—some still living.Broken relationships never again to mend,Broken promises and trust.
Tears that fall, seeming never to end,Sighs, the sound of the hopeless trying to hold on.Where did he go? Where did she go?Questions never to be answered.
Alone in my room, I hearA full-blown day party at a neighbor’s—Maybe a birthday or Christening.Wrong. Christening’s would be quieter.
I hear laughter, sounds of joy,Shouts of excitement.Mind you, I even hear the steps of dancersAs they sway their hips, throw their arms,And execute calculated steps on the dance floorTo that trendy music taking over the airwaves.Lomo Lomo, they call it?
But I am not jealous for not having been invited.Still, I cannot rejoice with them,I cannot feel with them,The momentary happiness they feel.
Because sitting here, alone with me,
In this room— is a broken heart.This heart—Not only broken but also hopeful—Still praying for what seemsUndoubtedly shattered,With no assurance of repairOr even the possibility.
All this broken heart can feelIs pain for all the broken hearts —
On the dance floor at my neighbor's house.How many broken dreams are hopingTo live this temporary fantasy permanently,Only to return to harsh realities?How many live life untrustinglyBecause someone who had their hearts broke their trust,And never acknowledged their hurt?
How many broken hearts are swayingTo the beat of trendy music,Holding onto a temporary fantasy of joy and excitement?
That’s all this broken heart can think,Even as it acknowledges the upbeat and vibrant rhythm of that trendy song,It cannot yet bring itselfTo derive happiness from what is supposed to be joyful.
Not yet. Not yet, but maybe soon.Just like other broken hearts are healed,Others yet to be broken,Others healing,And some that have built walls around themselves.
This broken heart may one day heal yet.It may heal soon.It may heal and build a wall around it's self,Or may not.
Whatever the case,I hope this heart can grab  The fleeting opportunities to let go and let God.Allowing the hips of the being it resides inTo sway to the tempo of that trendy song.The happiness may be fleeting,But must sadness be held onto,Especially when it does a good jobOf staying on its own?
This broken heart thinks about all the broken hearts out there.“I am with you,” she says.“This is life, and we will live it.”

content.title: I Know the Difference
content.raw_content:
Ever loved someone?
I ask gently—
because with me,
it feels like I am your first language,
and you are still learning how to speak.
You reach for me
with uncertain hands,
counting steps
where I have already learned to run.
And I stand here—
heart seasoned by the sweetness of being chosen,
by a love that did not hesitate,
did not whisper,
did not ask permission to bloom.
So tell me—
what is this we are building?
Because your “trying”
feels like tiptoeing around something sacred,
while I have known what it means
to be held without caution.
And I wonder…
if staying here
means shrinking the memory
of a love that once met me fully.
Still—
I wait.
Not out of need,
but out of grace.
I give time its quiet chance
to prove you capable of depth.
But hear me—
even if one day
you arrive with grand gestures
and borrowed courage,
I will know.
I will know
if it grew from a heart
that finally chose me,
or from one
that simply learned
how to pretend.

content.title: The Day After Forever
content.subtitle: He Showed Me the Moon, Then Left Me in Ruins
content.raw_content:
I often think of that conversation we had—the one where you spoke of believing, of loving truly, of not letting doubt sit where love should live. And I remember how I pressed the matter, how I insisted that sometimes a heart must be secured with doubt, if only so it may not be broken so easily again.

That conversation returns to me now and then, and each time it leaves me a little sadder, because it reminds me of the person I have become: a person who no longer knows how to believe, without trembling, in the complete and honorable love of another.

I have been hurt.I have been manipulated.I have been lied to.

Once, there was someone who promised me the world. He showed me the moon. He held my hand among the stars and lifted me high above the clouds. He was my loudest encouragement, my strongest support. He spoke of me as though I were rare, as though my life and my potential were things of wonder, things to be protected, things to be praised. I saw him in almost divine light. I never doubted him—not once. I could  never even make room for doubt, because he gave me no reason to. He showed me his love. He told me his love. He lived it, or so I believed.

He handled my heart with such care. He made me feel like the queen of his life.

And then one day, he dropped it.

He let it shatter into a million pieces and left me there as though I had meant nothing at all—as though I were no more than a pauper at the gates of a kingdom I had once been promised. Only the day before, he had pledged the world to me. He had spoken allegiance. He had called forever by my name. And then the very next day, he said I should forget everything he had ever said—that he had said it, yes, but he could retract it.

And now you come along.

Not loud.Not showy.Not wrapped in grand declarations.

And unfortunately, I like you.

That is where my struggle begins: between liking you and refusing to make a spectacle of my own heart; between leaning toward what I feel and holding myself back because perhaps you do not like me nearly as much. Perhaps you do like me, but not enough. Not in the way I would need. Not in the way your silence has yet to disprove.

So every day I remind myself to be careful.

Because my soul and I are coming from a place so delicate that even now I can still hear the sound of what was broken. The jewel of my existence was once shattered into a million pieces—without care, without grace, without love.

And from such a place, you ask me to trust you blindly?

content.raw_content:
SCENE 1: HAPPY AND BUSTLING FAMILY

AT RISE: (Scene opens on a well-decorated living room.)

Mr. Ismanu and his family mime laughing and talking about random things, they are in a celebratory mood; it’s one of those days. MAMUNA

Brother, your wife is endowed o; I wish I was as endowed as her. (They all laugh, except that Reverend’s laughter seems discordant and suspicious, conflicted by what he had witnessed, he excuses himself.)

REVEREND

I have some important things to take care of. (Lights flicker and go out, coming back on almost immediately to reveal the next scene.)

SCENE 2: VOICES TORMENTING THE GENDERLESS PERSON

(Dressed in black with a black mask to shield the actor’s identity; moving vigorously across the stage as if to get away from voices amidst quiet whimpers for help.)

VOICES

(Voices of every kind.)You are a horrible-terrible person! You low-life wretch! What kind of a person are you? Go find yourself a shameless being! I am ashamed to be called your mother! Woman, who is the father of that abomination?! I never knew you! I can’t leave with the fact that we are siblings! How dare you do that to the innocent girl . . . you shameless demon . . . Why introduce her into hell and not burn alone you devil?! You will never be accepted anywhere! Change your mind, change your life, and come back to your senses you despicable being! What have you done to my sister? Shame on you! What have you done to my sister? Shame on you! What have you done to my sister?!!!!!!!!!! (The last voice echoes deafeningly until the actor shouts to interrupt it and quietly the female and male voices deliver the next line while the actor  runs across the stage and into the audience  hesitantly as though imploring them, but also too scared . . . he doesn’t get dangerously close and  moves away quickly back onto the stage.)

ACTOR

(Standing center stage down, a male voice  speaks/echoes …teary, broken, and discouraged.) I just need help, love, care, and acceptance, don’t judge me...

(A female voice speaks/echoes …teary, broken, and feeling dejected.)I need your help, acceptance, love, care …  (Both voices.)…and your acceptance

(The actor falls to the floor with one knee on  the floor and face in hands and completely  covered in a show of despair, abrupt and  deafening silence follows, and lights flicker just  enough to allow the actor to exit us and allow  the next scene.)

SCENE 3: FAMILY MEETING

Trouble brewing… (The Reverend stands by the sofa, with enough light illuminating him and the sofa (not too bright though) and darkness around him.)

REVEREND

(Disdainfully but cautiously)Hello…(Pause…)  …you must come to my house today; today is the day I will prove myself and my accusations. Right beneath my roof, ah, this abomination will not continue! (He slumps into the sofa and echoes  desperation.)Mmhhm…(Sighs loudly in response, lights brighten as if to depict day break and he calls out to his daughter.

REVEREND

Shiela! Sheilaaaa!!!(Pause)Sheilaaaaaa!!(Sheila rushes into the room disheveled but it goes unnoticed.)Sheila, inform your mother to prepare to welcome our visitors  this afternoon, I am going out.(Several lights flicker once and go off abruptly, come on almost immediately to reveal an elderly man taking his seat with the other members of Reverend’s family. They all settle down, all members of the family including the two children. Then Reverend speaks…)

REVEREND

This is it…(Lights on them as they mime having an intense discussion, the elder intermittently shaking his head vigorously either in denial or acceptance. As this conversation goe on, the FIVE MINUTES SCENE will be going on with voices and everything.

SUGGESTION: This could take place on a partitioned stage or better still take place after SCENE 2.)When the FIVE MINUTES SCENE ends, that end of the stage darkens and full light and focus is placed on the EMERGENCY FAMILY MEETING as it continues with voices.)

Scene continues…

SCENE 4: FIVE MINUTES SCENE

Voices in the dark

(Both actors are dressed in black including a black mask in a dimly lit room (just enough so their movement can be seen, much left to the imagination though); a sofa in the center stage, on and around which action occurs. Sound does much to create moods ranging from yearning to agitation, to fear, then anger.)

FIRST WOMAN

I have missed you so much…

SECOND WOMAN

I am getting tired of hiding our love affair from everyone.  Sometimes I wish I could stand on the rooftop and proclaim my love to you...shout it out to all who have ears to hear.

FIRST WOMAN

(Erotic, low-pitch tone)

Yes, but first come sit with me, come rest your head on my bosom I have missed you more intensely than I can bear.

SECOND WOMAN

How I wish I had met you before, before him and now like a thief I sneak into the house that should have been mine anytime I need  rest.

My dear, come let's rest in each other’s arms, for the night rolls by quickly, we might lose it before we even begin.

Come here to me; let me kiss you passionately better than he ever has... (Passionately in each other’s arms, lips locked).

(Amidst moans…)This is the business I like to get down to... (Two minutes later).

FIRST WOMAN

(Softly and agitatedly)I hear movement...

SECOND WOMAN

You hear nothing love... (Both hear a subdued wimp of someone in pain and run silently and quickly into hiding, staying there for so long not knowing how many minutes had passed.)

SECOND WOMAN

(Quietly) Do you think they saw us?

FIRST WOMAN

(More agitated)I told you not to let us do it here. It’s unwise; it could have been in your bedroom.

SECOND WOMAN

(Quietly)Yes, but you should know that I want to destroy this safe haven of a lie you have and keep you all to myself. (Hearing more movement).

Ssshhhh, quiet… (They stay quiet for a while longer)

SECOND WOMAN

Good let's go to my room, no one saw us; come let us finish this song of love we sing each other.

(Irritated)No! (Quietly)I would go back to my room, lest we are caught and open up the full horrors of hell upon ourselves.

What now?!(Angrily but quietly)

I love you.

I love you too.(Goes away)

SCENE 5: FAMILY MEETING CONTINUES

REVEREND

No o! Please my husband, let’s talk about this, it is all a misunderstanding… someone is trying to destroy our marriage…someone is…

You two have brought me shame unthinkable!

Reverend calm down, that is why I am here, this is why you called me here, to talk about the matter, to understand how it started and how to end it for the continuity of the family. Think about the children, this might just be a test Reverend.

REVEREND

(Interrupts)If it is a test, then I have failed!!!! Out of my house you perverted, bed-sharing, degenerate harlots…out!

MRS. MARGARET

Honey…erm…your sister is just jealous of our union, she is trying to destroy our beautiful family, don’t let her evil plans work…

MAMUNA

Erheh? Is that so? I have been quiet all this while because I am used to these things. I have suffered being an outcast everywhere I have found myself, even from my own family. No one cares about me, society hates me, but I will not be quiet and watch you lie Missus. Who is it that wants to destroy your home; I thought you said you loved me? Coward and now…

REVEREND

Don’t honey me; Jezebel from the pit of hell… is this what you want your children to emulate? Your daughter?!

SCENE 6: THE ROKI FAMILY AT THE ISMANU’S HOUSE

(Sudden terrible and angry pounding at the door of the Ismanu’s startles everyone resulting in a moment of quiet till Reverend speaks out.)

Who is it that wants to break my door? Come in, it is open. (Madam Rita Roki, a member of Reverend Ismanu’s church, her husband who rarely visits the church, and their only daughter Marilyn who goes to school with Sheila appear through the door. I am here to confront that deviant who introduced my only  innocent daughter Marilyn to the devil’s ways….

(Obviously shocked speaks)There is no deviant or devil in my house, for your information  you are in a Reverend’s house please accord my presence and  house with some respect and explain why you are here again…

MR. ROKI

(Laughs disdainfully, deepening that angry murderous look.)  Reverend indeed! I did not come for you…(To himself)…that would be another time.(To Reverend)Once again I have come for that deviant and devil that has  ruined my daughter’s life…

REVEREND ISMANU

(More to himself.)I have one devil here, oh no two…(Looking at his wife and sister.)

MR. ROKI

(To his daughter and pointing to Sheila) Is it that the girl who introduced you? (Marilyn is hesitant)Don’t waste my time…

(He bellows angrily. This frightens Marilyn  who begins crying.)

MARILYN

(Pointing to Sheila amidst frightened tears, probably rethinking her life.)Yes, it’s that girl, Sheila…

She initiated me at school and now I don’t like boys…

What is she talking about?(To no one in particular.)

SCENE 1: JEFFERSON'S HOUSE

(Water closet flushes, footsteps, a click as the light is, and the sound of brewing coffee)

(Phone rings)

Jefferson

(He answers) Hello! Yes Lawyer Ntim, (Pause) I have been busy and have been unable to visit him in the hospital. (Pause) Why do you keep repeating that I had to visit him? (Pause, sounding angrier) It is too early to have this talk Lawyer Ntim, I do not like that man and nothing you say is going to make me visit him. But (Pause) why do you keep saying that I “had” to (stresses had’) visit him, you sound like my visit to him is no longer needed. (Long Pause) He is dead? (Not sounding the least remorseful)Oh he is dead! (Sounds quite unmoved, he clears his throat). (Pause) He died last week? (Pause). . . And why am I now finding out? (Pause)  You tried calling me . . . (Pause) Oh yes, I thought you were calling to insist on me visiting him (Pause) and you called several times yesterday too (Pause) Ah yes, I was busy and could not return the calls. (Pause) His will reading is today? (Pause) Oh! (Sounds very enthusiastic). Mmm, let me check the time (Pause) it’s 8am. (Pause) I will surely be there 2 pm prompt.

SCENE 2: MR. OTI'S MANSION

(The sound of audible chattering coupled with some quiet whispers which dies down as Lawyer Ntim begins to address those present.)

Lawyer Ntim

(Shuffles some papers). Good afternoon Ladies and Gentlemen of the Oti Family.

(Varying responses of good afternoons). Thanks for making it everyone for the gathering today. And as we have all been made aware when you were informed of this meeting, we are gathered here today for the Will reading of Mr. Oti . . . we proceed with no delay. (Varying responses of ‘great’ and ‘okay’).

Now to matters. . . Mr. Oti wants you to know that he deeply cares and loves you all and hopes that the wealth he leaves you can help you establish your lives even better than it is today. (Clears his throat and pauses before he continues) Mr. Julian Oti is bequeathed the Sunrays Estate situated on 1,500 acres of land located at Trassaco Valley and 4 Regan hotels located in Awoshie, Ofankor, Nyanyanu, and Weija.

(Chattering begins undertone and ceases when the Lawyer begins speaking again). (Shuffling paper) Serwaa Oti is bequeathed the 750 acres of land located in Santase as well as the remaining 4 Regan hotels located in Lapaz, Kwashieman, Dansoman, and East Legon. That would be all . . .

Jefferson

(Butts in sharply) And what of me?!

Lawyer

Yes, Mr. Jefferson . . .(Pause). (Shuffles through his documents)

. . . I was getting there. (Pause) Mr. Oti in his will stated that you could have all he had bequeathed you only if you’d satisfy a clause.

Jefferson

(Impatiently) Wait what clause?

Lawyer Ntim

What did Mr. Oti tell you about your paternity?

Jefferson

(Impatiently)What kind of question is that, Mr. Lawyer Ntim? Do not waste my precious time, (huffs) read away the will and let me know my share of the properties that father of mine left me(rashly and harshly). (mumbles of eeiis)

Jefferson

(Claps back) What?!

(Pause then angrily) What is there to tell me about my paternity other than the fact that Mr. Oti was an irresponsible father who has thought that leaving me with my mother and providing for me financially whilst cutting me away from his immediate family was the way to be a good father? To imagine that I got to know about him only when I was in my teens, I hate him!

Julian

(Calmly but with authority) Do not talk about our father like that.

Jefferson

And what if I do? (Menacingly)

Lawyer Ntim

(Butts in)Gentlemen! There is no need for this right now. We are in mourning and we should not soil the name of the dead. (Pause) Mr. Jefferson, (Pause) Mr. Oti before his demise wanted you to know that he was not your biological father. . .

Jefferson

What?! What are you talking about? The audacity!

Julian

Yes, and we know, father told us, (short Pause) he also warned us to never let you know. He only decided to tell . . .

Jefferson

Will you shut up?!

Lawyer Ntim

Enough! (He rants out the following)Your mother was unfaithful to Mr. Oti, they divorced when he found out the truth about your paternity. He out of a kind heart, decided to continue to play a part in your upbringing financially and even promised your late mother to do so till you were of age and able to stand on your own and fend for yourself. Your mother was supposed to tell you the truth of your paternity but according to Mr. Oti she never did, it seemed. All he ever wanted to do was to support your upbringing as he once thought of you as his own. But you grew up and hated him with a passion.

Jefferson

I had every right to, and besides I don’t believe what you are claiming.

Lawyer Ntim

It doesn’t matter if you believe me or not (calmly)I am saying that, because you were unable to fulfill the clause which was to visit Mr. Oti and allow him to tell you the truth and make amends which he wanted to  so badly on his death bed, (pause)the properties which otherwise would have been yours will be sold and money donated to the poor.

Jefferson

(Screams)No! You cannot do this!

SCENE 3: JEFFERSON'S HOUSE

(All is quiet as he broods alone drinking a bottle of vodka)

Jefferson

Oh, oh, oh . . .! (Slurred speech) Oh boy! I messed up big time! I have been angry with my dad all these years thinking he didn’t love me as much as his other children but he wasn’t even my biological father.

I’ve lost it all . . . (he sobs). Nooooooooooooooooooo (screams like something out of a horror movie).

THE END

A deep voice (that of the narrator, as airily as possible) seeps through the night and echoes, “And so it happened…” (followed by the crackling of thunder, and a sudden quiet, followed again by the chirping of birds and the croaking of frogs ushering in the first Act).

ACT 1: THE SHRINE (AT DAWN)

This scene opens on a shrine just before the break of dawn, poorly lit with a kerosene lantern or two, a fetish priest and an older man, they seem to be having an intense moment as the priest keeps looking into a pot and shaking his whisk over it alongside shaking his head in disbelief. The priest continues to shake his whisk over the pot anytime he looks into it as if trying to change whatever he is seeing to something else. Finally, when it seems nothing will change, he looks up to the older man and says gloomily.

Priest: The gods are tight -lipped, the picture they show is blur and they offer no explanation for the incurable ailment of your wife’s child aside letting you know that the answer you seek lies in the bosom of the child’s mother.

Opanyin: Please….

Priest: Sssshhh... listen to what the gods have to say first. The gods say that you are asleep but your legs are outside…. mmm....mm, they say that you must go and put your house in order because by a single gunshot breaking through the dawn and welcoming the first rays of the morning star the end shall be signified.

Opanyin Asem: What does all this mean Nana? Nana I am tired of parables and riddles. The gods should be fair with me, I have served them in faithfulness all these years. Please Nana plead with them on my behalf to tell me something, to at least give me the assurance that my son will live and not die.

Priest: Humph, humph… (Shaking his whisk over the pot and looking into it again) The gods say that no son coming from your loins will die because… (three gunshots are heard in quick succession startling them.

Opanyin Asem: Eeeii Nana, who could be hunting at this hour when I the greatest hunter has not yet sharpened my bows and prepared my gun for the jungle, that sounded unnatural though…

Priest: (laughs thoughtfully) Yes Opanyin, the gods speak to us all the time and in every way they can, the question to ask is, do we hear, and do we understand when we hear? Opanyin the gods have spoken (as he says this he stands up, picks his pot and whisk, turns around and retreats back into the sanctuary of the shrine leaving Opanyin seated in confusion, as he gets up to leave too the lights dim on him).

ACT 2: MARKET SQUARE (IN THE AFTERNOON)

Lights fill in on the local palm wine seller surrounded by the local palm drinkers, occupying themselves with talks of what goes on in every local’s bedroom as they sip their delicious palm wine and plunge more and more into debt with the palm wine seller, Maame Akua walks in.

Maame Akua: (to the palm wine seller) Good afternoon Auntie Esi

Auntie Esi: (looks up and on seeing Maame Akua responds disdainfully with a show of scorn) Erherh madam, to what do we owe this visit this hot afternoon, why has the bat come out of her dark place?

Man: (Clears his throat loudly) Erh Maame Palmwine, easy on the woman, she has greeted you nicely, just respond equally, if not equally just respond at least and hear her out.

Man 2: You say what? Let her accost her, Maame Palmwine go on, when she came in she saw only you to be worthy of her greetings.

Maame Akua: I am sorry o, Good afternoon.

All (except Auntie Esi): Good afternoon

Man 3: Now tell us what you came here to tell us, I am listening…

Man 1: Ah, and who said she came to talk to you, leave the poor woman alone.

Maame Akua: Actually I came to look for my brother, have you seen Awusie?

Man 3: Awusie, who is Awusie? In fact, who is your brother? You mean your husband?

Maame Akua: (looks taken aback, uncomfortable and plays with her clothes untying it to tie again)

Man 1: Will you shut up! Don’t you know her husband Opanyin Asem, the most respected hunter in this village? Have you ever seen him sit and drink with…?

Man 3: let me continue for you…low life, jobless and aimless people like us?

Man 1: Mmm. I was going to put it rather nicely but you have a point anyway…

Auntie Esi: (standing now) Oh yes, he has a point!

Man 2: Hey hey hey, Auntie Esi, don’t insult us or else we will leave your drink for you and come back for it tomorrow.

Auntie Esi: Sorry o I didn’t mean to bruise the ego that I didn’t know was there in the first place. Now let me address this woman... Maame Akua, you can leave now, as you can see Awusie is not here and your presence here is undesirable…

All: eeiiii Undesirable to who? (they all say together, look at each other’s faces and start laughing hysterically)

Auntie Esi: …to me

Man 3: Aaaaah okay, but not to us o, this woman turns heads everywhere she goes, see as she is turning my head (he looks away from Maame Akua and turns his head to look at her with his free hand slowly) and the other two men say the same and follow suit together “See the way she is turning my head” as they turn their heads to look at her again and they all laugh again.)

Maame Akua: Please if you see him…

Man 2: Oh there he is (he points to Awusie the drunk who approaches them unsteadily).

Maame Akua: Oh where is he, where is he? (She turns around and rushes to Awusie, grabs his arm and pulls him away quickly with force) Oh thank you, thank you (she says as she pulls Awusie away with her).

Auntie Esi: Look at her (she chuckles and takes and seat).

All: (Turn to look at her and continue to stare as she sits then they start talking).

Man 3: (to the others) Do you know why Auntie Esi doesn’t like Maame Akua?

Man 1: We know but tell us

Man 2: Yes, go ahead

Man 3: Opanyin Asem had eyes for her until he set his eyes on Maame Akua and he never looked back.

Man 2: Yes o Auntie Esi is jealous, she is a very jealous woman

Man 1: Yes, I told you, didn’t I?

Auntie Esi: Hey hey hey, you men will not gossip about me like I am not even here

All: Sorry o

Man 3: We will gossip like you are here

Man 2: Erherh, do you know Opanyin Asem’s son is critically ill?

Man 3: You mean Papa Awusie’s son?

Man 1: Ssshh, will you shut up? Don’t let anyone hear that from you ever again

Man 3: If it is the truth should I not say it? He is my friend I know…

Man 1: Shut up!

Man 2: Eeeeeiii eeeeeiiii ei ei ei ei ei (loudly)

Man 1: What is it?

Man 2: So it is true? I have heard the rumours, I have seen the resemblance, tell me more

Auntie Esi: Yes, tell us more (very interested now).

Man 3: So…

Man 1: Shut up! You Gossip!

Man 3: (startled but recovers quickly) ah but do you know what I want to say?

All: What?!

Man 3: Erherh, Auntie Esi wanted to marry Opanyin Asem, we must look into it, she probably has something to do with the child’s ailment.

Auntie Esi: Herh! You will be careful wai (points her finger at him threatingly) or …

Man 1: Or what?

Auntie Esi: I…

Man 2: It’s okay, it’s okay, let’s not fight. Maame Palmwine please sit down and allow us men to gossip in peace and men let us gossip like she is here okay

All: Okay

Man 2: (To Man 3) so what were you saying about Auntie Esi again?

Man 3: Erherh, so they say that Auntie Esi ….

Auntie Esi: Herh!! (Takes off her slipper and stretches her hand menacingly, the men all sway to the side to avoid the impact and they freeze.)

Lights dim out

ACT 3: OPANYIN ASEM’S HOUSE (PAST MID-NIGHT)

On the compound lies a young child, nine years old dying and covered wholly in a cloth, his head on his mother’s lap (Maame Akua) who sits on the mat too, and a man (Awusie) sprinkling some concoction on the boy from the crown of his head to the sole of his feet with some leaves as he mumbles some words only stopping once a while to catch his breath.

Maame Akua: Aha do it just like I told you, we have to do this till the break of dawn

Awusie: Eeei Maame Akua, do you want to kill me…why, won’t we sleep? I am tired o

Maame Akua: (threatingly) if you ever say that again …

Awusie: (who had knelt to rest gets up quickly and continues the incantations and sprinkling)

Just then Opanyin Asem walks into his compound and cannot believe what meets his eyes. Maame Akua and Awusie oblivious of Opanyin’s entry go on uninterrupted until he speaks.

Opanyin Asem: (He regains his composure and barks out to Awusie) what are you doing here drunkard and in your right senses too? Interesting… (To Maame Akua) what is he doing here in my house and with my son? How dare you bring this ingrate here in my absence and what is he even doing here at this time of the day? When I go about seeking a cure for our dying son, this is what you do? Get out of my house you ingrate!

Maame Akua: (Being quiet all this while, snaps out of it and tearily and quietly says) the boy he dies, his life ebbs out of him slowly but steadily, I had to do something, I had to take action, he dies my husband, he dies…

Opanyin Asem: I will not be insulted in my own house, no not in my house; (He bellows) get out!

Awusie is hesitant, not stopping for once what he is doing but slowly this time, and he keeps looking at Maame Akua like he is scared (which he is) and as if seeking justification for still being there.

Opanyin Asem: (Noticing how Awusie keeps looking at Maame Akua like he cannot leave even if he wanted to, grows quiet momentarily and says quietly as if an understanding is dawning on him) wait what do you mean by you had to take action, you had to do something (to Maame Akua) like this is not what I have been doing for the past year, every single day and night ever since this boy’s sickness began. Ever since that native doctor from that other town told us our boy had just a short time to live and these may be his last having been destined so due to the circumstance of his birth, I have not eaten, I have not slept and you are a witness, I have lived like a wild animal in the forest hoping the gods of our fathers and my great hunting gun would have mercy on me and appear to me with a cure but nothing so far. And you sit there with your brother and label me irresponsible? That you a woman would go out of your way and seek a cure for my son with that ingrate of a brother behind my back? Maame Akua I am tired, I am worn and feel like a shadow of myself, please insult me not in my house.

Maame Akua: My Lord, my husband, the father of the child, he cannot go… (She quickly clasps her hand over her mouth looking hysterically frightened, she quickly snaps out of it when it looks like Opanyin Asem does not register what she just said and continues carefully and more pleadingly) he cannot go or the boy dies, my child dies.

Opanyin Asem: Your child? (He rushes into the room)

(The following dialogue ensues quickly and tensely)

Awusie: Maame Akua, your husband hates me…

Maame Akua: …and for good reason…

Awusie: I must go for he is wrath with anger; he will find out; this could turn out bad. Who knows what he might do now?

Maame Akua: You will go nowhere, you coward who cannot be brave even to save your own life (She spits out but quietly to avoid being overheard) this boy must live, and you will remain here to keep him alive! And here I thought you were glad to have a son you will never have because no woman in her right mind would marry you talk less of giving you a son, you drunkard, you will stay here and go nowhere.

Opanyin Asem rushes out with his hunting gun and points it at Awusie who throws the leaves and concoction he is holding away in frenzy and escapes amidst screams for his dear life.

Maame Akua: (She carefully but quickly lifts the boy’s head from her laps and settles it on the mat and throws herself at the feet of Opanyin Asem, clutching him tightly and wailing). The boy he dies, daddy, Opanyin, he dies, the boy, he dies, our son (the lights go off immediately she speaks the last words “our son”)

ACT 4: OPANYIN ASEM’S COMPOUND (PAST MID-NIGHT)

(Lights out) Opanyin Asem and Maame Akua walk away from the center stage with the boy still lying there and walk in opposite direction to the ends of the stage to have a monologue and dialogue altogether.

In the stark darkness two spotlights show on each person: a blue spotlight for Opanyin Asem (where blue indicates protection and loyalty as well as depression, the darkness of the night, doubt and emotional distance) and a yellow spotlight for Maame Akua (where yellow indicates a traitor and infidelity)

Opanyin Asem: (Solemnly; indicating pride yet sadness altogether) I am Opanyin Asem, the greatest hunter this village has ever seen apart from our great ancestor Surobiribi who killed a royal python with his bare hands. I also have killed a lion which terrorized our people, kept them from their farms and killed many, after three days in the forest when many thought I was already dead for going on such a quest to free my people, I returned with the head of gyata. I have earned my place among our ancestors, I am feared amongst my fellow hunters and villagers alike but for some time now rumors have turned me into a laughing stalk, they call me an impotent caretaker of a taboo child; people point fingers at me and make fun of me, where they would previously have looked away reverently when I looked in their direction they now stare me down with scornful eyes, I must say some filled with pity. I am a man; a man takes pity from no one. Or is it for my son; is it for my family I ask? But there is this man who calls himself my wife’s brother, in his drunken stupor he claims to father my child; this he has dared to say to my face several times. I do not speak of it, I do not think of it or at least I try, it is unimaginable, not in my house, it cannot happen; he knows not what he speaks…for Kwame my little boy is blood of my blood and bone of my bone, from my loins he came forth…he is a true son of his father and that is without question, me.

Maame Akua: My Lord, my husband, you came for me when no one would. You paid the bride price on my head and treated me with respect when I was a trophy to others. I was wild in my youth, just a couple of years back. Now I am learned, now I am experienced. With my great beauty, I felt loved, when men would come trooping at my feet; I thought they were showing me love but I was just a fling for the moment. I got involved with a married man from the city, his wife came to this village when she found out about me, she told me she felt sorry for me and though I might not have known he was a married man she had placed a very potent curse on any woman who would sleep with her husband. The curse said that woman would never have a legitimate child with her husband when married. She created no scene except to say what she said to me. I was young, I was hopeful it was just a scare, until we married fourteen years ago and I couldn’t birth you a child after five years of being married. Then like in a dream the words of this woman came back to me.

Opanyin Asem: You never told me of this curse, I am no stranger in this village. I knew of your wild past, but I loved you when I got to know the person under all the criticism. My first wife’s death made me believe I would not love again but not until I got to know you.

Maame Akua: You never would have married me! I knew you were without a child, people said you were impotent; I doubt you would have wanted to marry a woman with such an extra baggage.

Opanyin Asem: Assumption has always been one of man’s greatest weaknesses…

Maame Akua: I had to do what I had to do, after five years of a childless marriage and the taunts from your family telling you they told you so. And all the people who would laugh at me and tell me I married an impotent man. Seeing you couldn’t stay at home but would spend days in the forest putting yourself in harm’s way, I had to act fast but I did so stupidly.

Opanyin Asem: I have never been an impotent man, my first wife was barren and I knew this but for the great love I had for her never did I say a word. She hoped I would get the child I always wanted with another woman but (shakes his head disappointedly) ...you should have told me; we would have found a way…together.

Maame Akua: One of the many nights you spent in the forest, Awusie came by to comfort me and….

Opanyin Asem: And what?! (Moves quickly to the center as if going to her but stops at the center up) What is this you say Maame?

Maame Akua: I had to… the curse (Rushes to kneel at his feet holding his cloth imploringly and weeping)

Opanyin Asem: What curse woman? Such a taboo under my very roof (Shakes himself from her grip and pushes her away. He angrily walks to the center stage to join the boy; stands exactly where he stood when the first act transitioned into this next act; as Maame Akua remains in her fallen position; all the while the only lights on are the two spotlights which move with them as they move on stage)

Maame Akua: (She gets up and rushes to him kneeling once again like at the end of the first scene and continues to implore as she weeps) please Opanyin (At these words the spot lights go off (leaving just a momentary darkness, then the lights come on a dim orange).

Opanyin Asem: This is how you repay me Maame…

Maame Akua: We can fix this… (She runs to check the boy’s pulse and gets back at Opanyin Asem’s feet) the boy dies, he pulses crawls like a dying tortoise…it’s almost not there…there is still time, it can be fixed.

Opanyin Asem: Fix what? You insulted me, my lineage, my house, my existence…you’ve made a taboo of my household.

Maame Akua: Please…

Opanyin Asem: No!

Maame Akua: The boy, he is not at fault, he dies…

Opanyin Asem: And so do we all… (lights turn a dim red and he pushes her violently away from himself and fires a single shot at her killing her instantly). (He goes to check the boy’s pulse and breath, he covers the boy’s eyes and kisses him on the forehead bidding him farewell and he says) this is through no fault of yours.

(He walks to the center of the stage and to the audience says) like the native doctor, this dawn said, “By a single gunshot breaking through the dawn and welcoming the first rays of the morning star the end shall be signified. (At this he picks some leaves from his pocket, kneels, lifts them to the sky puts them into his mouth, and begins to chew, he isn’t even halfway through when he falls on his side dead).

The Narrator’s voice comes through solemnly: The break of old dawn and the eyes of ancient sun see once again the folly of man end in three lifeless bodies of a once lively household; a father, a mother, and even more sad a child.

THE END

And here I thought you were glad to have a son you will never have because no woman in her right mind would marry you talk less of giving you a son, you drunkard, you will stay here and go nowhere.
Opanyin Asem rushes out with his hunting gun and points it at Awusie who throws the leaves and concoction he is holding away in frenzy and escapes amidst screams for his dear life.

Maame Akua: (She carefully but quickly lifts the boy’s head from her laps and settles it on the mat and throws herself at the feet of Opanyin Asem, clutching him tightly and wailing). The boy he dies, daddy, Opanyin, he dies, the boy, he dies, our son (the lights go off immediately she speaks the last words “our son”)
ACT 4: OPANYIN ASEM’S COMPOUND (PAST MID-NIGHT)

(Lights out) Opanyin Asem and Maame Akua walk away from the center stage with the boy still lying there and walk in opposite direction to the ends of the stage to have a monologue and dialogue altogether.

In the stark darkness two spotlights show on each person: a blue spotlight for Opanyin Asem (where blue indicates protection and loyalty as well as depression, the darkness of the night, doubt and emotional distance) and a yellow spotlight for Maame Akua (where yellow indicates a traitor and infidelity)

Opanyin Asem: (Solemnly; indicating pride yet sadness altogether) I am Opanyin Asem, the greatest hunter this village has ever seen apart from our great ancestor Surobiribi who killed a royal python with his bare hands. I also have killed a lion which terrorized our people, kept them from their farms and killed many, after three days in the forest when many thought I was already dead for going on such a quest to free my people, I returned with the head of gyata. I have earned my place among our ancestors, I am feared amongst my fellow hunters and villagers alike but for some time now rumors have turned me into a laughing stalk, they call me an impotent caretaker of a taboo child; people point fingers at me and make fun of me, where they would previously have looked away reverently when I looked in their direction they now stare me down with scornful eyes, I must say some filled with pity. With my great beauty, I felt loved, when men would come trooping at my feet; I thought they were showing me love but I was just a fling for the moment. I got involved with a married man from the city, his wife came to this village when she found out about me, she told me she felt sorry for me and though I might not have known he was a married man she had placed a very potent curse on any woman who would sleep with her husband. The curse said that woman would never have a legitimate child with her husband when married. She created no scene except to say what she said to me. I was young, I was hopeful it was just a scare, until we married fourteen years ago and I couldn’t birth you a child after five years of being married. Then like in a dream the words of this woman came back to me.

Opanyin Asem: You never told me of this curse, I am no stranger in this village. I knew of your wild past, but I loved you when I got to know the person under all the criticism. My first wife’s death made me believe I would not love again but not until I got to know you.
Maame Akua: You never would have married me! I knew you were without a child, people said you were impotent; I doubt you would have wanted to marry a woman with such an extra baggage.
Opanyin Asem: Assumption has always been one of man’s greatest weaknesses…

Maame Akua: I had to do what I had to do, after five years of a childless marriage and the taunts from your family telling you they told you so. And all the people who would laugh at me and tell me I married an impotent man. Seeing you couldn’t stay at home but would spend days in the forest putting yourself in harm’s way, I had to act fast but I did so stupidly.

Opanyin Asem: I have never been an impotent man, my first wife was barren and I knew this but for the great love I had for her never did I say a word. She hoped I would get the child I always wanted with another woman but (shakes his head disappointedly) ...you should have told me; we would have found a way…together.
Maame Akua: One of the many nights you spent in the forest, Awusie came by to comfort me and….
Opanyin Asem: And what?! (Moves quickly to the center as if going to her but stops at the center up) What is this you say Maame?
Maame Akua: I had to… the curse (Rushes to kneel at his feet holding his cloth imploringly and weeping)

Opanyin Asem: What curse woman? Such a taboo under my very roof (Shakes himself from her grip and pushes her away. He angrily walks to the center stage to join the boy; stands exactly where he stood when the first act transitioned into this next act; as Maame Akua remains in her fallen position; all the while the only lights on are the two spotlights which move with them as they move on stage)

Maame Akua: (She gets up and rushes to him kneeling once again like at the end of the first scene and continues to implore as she weeps) please Opanyin (At these words the spot lights go off (leaving just a momentary darkness, then the lights come on a dim orange).
Opanyin Asem: This is how you repay me Maame…

Maame Akua: We can fix this… (She runs to check the boy’s pulse and gets back at Opanyin Asem’s feet) the boy dies, he pulses crawls like a dying tortoise…it’s almost not there…there is still time, it can be fixed.
Opanyin Asem: Fix what? You insulted me, my lineage, my house, my existence…you’ve made a taboo of my household.
Maame Akua: Please…
Opanyin Asem: No!
Maame Akua: The boy, he is not at fault, he dies…

Opanyin Asem: And so do we all… (lights turn a dim red and he pushes her violently away from himself and fires a single shot at her killing her instantly). (He goes to check the boy’s pulse and breath, he covers the boy’s eyes and kisses him on the forehead bidding him farewell and he says) this is through no fault of yours.

(He walks to the center of the stage and to the audience says) like the native doctor, this dawn said, “By a single gunshot breaking through the dawn and welcoming the first rays of the morning star the end shall be signified. (At this he picks some leaves from his pocket, kneels, lifts them to the sky puts them into his mouth, and begins to chew, he isn’t even halfway through when he falls on his side dead).

The Narrator’s voice comes through solemnly: The break of old dawn and the eyes of ancient sun see once again the folly of man end in three lifeless bodies of a once lively household; a father, a mother, and even more sad a child.
THE END

content.raw_content:
PHASE 1

YAAKROM (The Village)

(The stage is dimly lit. There is a tree center stage. A man dressed in an elaborate fetish priest garb stands in front of the tree and gazes at the night sky as if reading the stars. He is the Village’s fetish priest. He speaks…).

Village Priest: The time of life is as it should be, and from the beginning of one’s journey on this earth till the return to the land of the ancestors,  Odomankoma requires that each mortal soul runs the errand for which he was sent to the earth. (He jumps high and lands on one knee  on the ground, with his staff in hand) Odomankoma! Odomankoma!  Oboade3!!! We shall dance to the rhythm you play, for it is in your rhythm the melody of our lives we find.

Lights fade out and fade in slowly to reveal the next scene after the village priest has exited the stage.

PHASE 2

FLASHBACK

Happened five years ago.

IN THE COURTYARD OF THE HOUSE

Yellow spotlight fades in on the downstage left (alternatively blue spotlight).

Midwife: The baby is born, oh see such a beauty! Yewura behold your daughter,  your firstborn.

Yewura: My baby, my daughter mine … (baby’s cries cease) Midwife… Midwife: Abawa, take the child let me clean up Mama…

Yewura: No, no, midwife the baby, she is not crying, is she breathing? Midwife: (on her knees and cleaning Mama up, looks up to Yewura). Mama: (raises her neck) What? (Sound and Light should work to create a heavy and heart-wrenching atmosphere).  (They all freeze, the spotlight either grows dim on them or fades out immediately). Blue spotlight fades in on the downstage right.

Yewura: She is in labour…

Midwife: Right on time I am …

Mama: … (Screams in pain) …

Yewura: Midwife hurry…

Midwife: Yes, yes, to work immediately… mama push, puuuush, push… (seeing the child’s head she smiles) … push mama…. (the child is delivered).

Yewura: … (Cannot contain the cocktail of emotions)

Midwife: Yewura, the baby is born, oh see such a beauty! Yewura behold your daughter, your first born…

Yewura: … (Takes the child) …my baby, my daughter…. midwife…she has stopped breathing?

Midwife: Abawa! (She stands up) No (in denial) …

Yewura: No…

Sound and Light should work to create a heavy and heart-wrenching atmosphere.  (They all freeze, the spotlight either grows dim on them or fades out immediately). The red spotlight fades in on center stage.

Yewura: She is in labor…. My wife….

Midwife: (exasperated) …yes, she is …

Yewura: Quick, see to her (amidst mama’s loud wailing) …

Midwife: (She gets to work, and a beautiful baby girl is born) Your baby Yewura…  (moves to hand over the baby to Yewura)….

Yewura: No! …(fumbles) No, no, I am sorry….

Midwife: I understand… Abawa takes the child…

Abawa: … (Takes the child) …

Yewura: … (Takes a peep at the baby in Abawa’s arms and sees the baby has stopped crying and breathing screams) …She is not breathing midwife!

Mama: (raises her head and gives a bloodcurdling scream and falls back crying loudly).

Sound and Light should work to create a heavy and heart-wrenching atmosphere.  (They all freeze, the spotlight either grows dim on them or fades out immediately).

The Priest appears on the left wing (spotlight on him and a soulful or enchanting tune playing) looks up into the skies and speaks…

Village Priest: I see … I read in the stars, the priestess…she is not ready to come ... she comes, and she goes, comes, and goes again. The heart of a mother cries out and the father looks on powerless… the priestess still choosing the worthy time…

He walks off stage and the spotlight fades out.

PHASE 3

TWO YEARS LATER

In a dream…

Mama: Priest, I greet you…

Village Priest: (Standing under the Boabab tree) My daughter the gods have heard your cry… next year by this time you will hear the continuous cry of a living child in your house but after that expect a message.

Next day…

Mama: (Singing a song happily as she sweeps the courtyard) …

Yewura: (walks to her) Mama, you look very cheerful this morning, tell me what the good news is. (Mama tells Yewura of her dream and they both go about their day happy and thankful to the gods, for such an encounter even in a dream is not one they take lightly).

PHASE 4

A YEAR LATER …

(Mama, Yewura, the midwife and Abawa are all singing praises to the gods for Mama’s successful delivery of a beautiful bouncing baby girl).

The village priest appears on the scene…

Village priest: (To them) The gods have spoken, and they have let come to pass…the child is chosen one of the gods…. she belongs to the gods and the gods will take for themselves what belongs to them after her eighth birthday… (he disappears).

PHASE 5

EIGHT YEARS LATER

IN THE COURTYARD OF THE HOUSE

Akua is seated on a stool as Mama braids her hair.

Akua: Mama I had a dream, and, in the dream, I was standing under a tree, it  was the big baobab tree in the middle of the village. But then mama, I  was just standing still…like I had nowhere to go, and like I came from no place and the feeling was like my beginning and end were right under the big baobab tree….

Mama: (interjects)………….…eei my daughter, full of tales this one, never a dull moment with you, it is either this or it is that …

Akua: Mama but that is not all, I wore my favorite dress, the one you gave me during the last yam festival, the blue dress with the white polka dots. I was barefooted though and holding… (She pauses to think,  recollecting what it was she was holding). Mama…it was a leaf… a yellow baobab leaf. I just stared at it …and stared at it …and stared at it…and…

Mama: …and what my child, what?!...

Akua: Nothing Mama…

Mama: Why nothing?

Akua: I was awakened when you came calling me to wake up because the rays of the sun had long kissed the horizon a blessed day Mama.

Mama: Okay…a very interesting dream that is. You have been quite a dreamer ever since you were little but thankfully most of your dreams have remained dreams as they should.

Akua: Erm mama, most? Have some others come true…?

Mama: … (Quickly interjecting) No my child, forgive my expression… not most but all your dreams have remained dreams as they ought to.

(A soft sound of wind is played and both Akua and Mama feel the sudden chill).

Akua: Eii Mama, it is cold outside…

Mama: Yes child, let’s continue this inside the house.

(Both get up and go inside).

(Lights fade out slowly as a dramatic sound or music is played).

PHASE 6

(Sitting outside the house in the moonlight, Mama, and Yewura her husband are deep in conversation speaking in a hushed tone, avoiding being overheard).

Yewura: What is it you are saying, woman?

Mama: I said our child has had another dream again

Yewura: And she told you about it?

Mama: …. Of course, she told me about it, that is why we are here in the first place, or have you forgotten?

Yewura: Oh no I haven’t. Just go ahead and tell me about it.

Mama: Hmm, she was wearing her favorite dress and standing under the big baobab tree, staring at a yellow leaf in her hand.

Yewura: And what happened afterward?

Mama: Nothing…

Yewura: …What do you mean nothing? Most certainly another action should have followed or?

Mama: (fidgeting with the ends of her clothes).

Yewura: What is it?

Mama: I interrupted her dream by waking her up.

Yewura: Eeei, I hope you remember the disaster that almost befell the Odua household because Akua was not able to tell you her complete dream of their younger son.

Mama: Yes, I do remember. How I couldn’t warn them to be extra careful with taking him to the farm with them the next day because Akua did not tell me…

Yewura: And she didn’t tell you because she did not dream it...

Mama: .... but only dreamed of them going to the farm and some strange gloom over their household which was interrupted by my waking her up…

Yewura: ... and how we agreed to allow Akua to wake up on her own accord in the mornings, lest we interrupt an ongoing prophecy from the gods….

Mama: Yes, my husband, I made a mistake, I needed her to go fetch some water for cooking…I forgot…

Yewura: ……. ...… and now we do not know how that dream ended, how do we protect the child or warn anyone who needs to be warned?

Mama: ...… (She gets up from her stool and starts pacing about slowly). My husband, our child is growing into her destiny and even hiding the fact that her dreams are prophecies does not stop her from dreaming, and neither does it stop her from sharing…

Yewura: Yes, my wife, it is as if she knows to not keep her dreams to herself for it could be the life or death of someone…anybody…

Mama: . … and I will continue to be the unordained messenger of the gods,  telling her dreams to those who need to hear it to order their steps and still hide the truth of her destiny from her…oh my husband, how I  wish the gods would let me keep this child…to leave my one and only child for me…to grow up and bear children like other women and make me a satisfied grandmother compensated with grandchildren for the children I never had.

Yewura: I wish that too, but the gods have their will, and they will have it no other way…. Akua is eight years old now…but she is not like any ordinary girl you know…she knows it…she feels it…and sometimes I  feel she can see into my soul when she looks me dead in the eyes…

Mama: You think she would know she is destined to be the Priestess of this land even though we have hidden it from her and are still trying….

Yewura: Woman…. shhhhhh (in resignation) we cannot win this war against the gods…we might have to allow the Village priest to take her in and train her as has been required of us since her birth…we will surely lose this…

Mama: No! The gods gave me this child, but they will not take her away from me…even if we will surely lose…I will keep fighting for my daughter…

my only child. The gods should pick another young maiden from the households of those who have many children….

Yewura: Calm down! We must be careful what we say and tone down, Akua may be asleep, but she might overhear us…we must tread carefully.

Mama: Hmm, can the gods be this wicked? After blessing me with the seed of the womb after eight years of childlessness, they turn around and proclaim her the chosen one…a priestess?!

(Unknown to them Akua is standing close to the door and overhearing their conversation having woken up some minutes ago and realizing her parents are outside).

Yewura: Hmmm, a priestess…

Mama: Hm, my child a priestess!

Akua: (She steps outside to her parents) A Priestess? Me?  Mama and Yewura: (Startled but recovered quickly) No my child! Not you!

Mama: Let’s go back inside Akua, you must go back to bed tomorrow is another day.

(They all go inside).

(Lights fade out and fade in to reveal the next and final scene).

PHASE 7

(Village Priest goes to the house of Mama and Yewura in the absence of their only child  Akua, who has gone to the stream to fetch some water).

Village Priest: (He enters the courtyard in a trance-like state, stands in the center, and speaks) The great baobab tree is the footstool of our ancestors and gods, whoever is connected stays green but he who is cut off withers.  Mmm, I see a withering in the land of the living, the handmaiden of the gods, where is she? Where is she, I ask you? You seek to keep her from her calling because you do not want to lose your only child, but you shall lose her nevertheless to withering or to the gods… and again the choice is yours! She will wither…mmm…I see a yellowing…yes … the East I see the eagle fly away with a leaf in its beak…it flies so quickly that the traces of green barely register on my very eyes. Then also, I see the vulture carrying a yellow leaf and it communes with the child’s soul. Be warned…be warned…be warned!!!

(Then in a gust of wind he disappears like he never was there).

(Mama and Yewura who have been hiding inside all this while come out of the house the instant they perceive the priest is gone).

Mama: Eei what did he mean? The yellow leaf …the withering… the baobab tree! Yewura: (He is pacing about anxiously) Quiet woman, let me think… Mama: Aha! It is the dream…. I remember it was her dream!

Yewura: That is what I fear, what it mean for our daughter is what I fear?

(Two young men rush into the courtyard carrying a convulsing Akua followed by a crowd of people).

Mama: Eei what happened to my daughter? Please put her here (She quickly shows them a mat to lay her daughter on).

Yewura: What happened to her? What happened to my daughter (He bellows)

First Man: She was coming back from the stream with her pot of water, chatting with her friends when …

Second Man: (continuing from where First Man ends) …when a vulture with a leaf in its beak flew right past her, she panicked, dropped her water pot, and fell to the ground convulsing…

First Man: (continues) and has not for a moment ceased convulsing…

Yewura: We need the Village Priest….!

(Yewura barely mentions the Village Priest when he appears with a gust of wind which dies down as suddenly as it appeared).

Village Priest: She must come with me if she is going to survive this. She must be dedicated to the gods, to live the life of a demigod… so the yellow leaf can be nurtured and flourish as green again, and the vulture shall be overtaken, as nature would have it by the eagle.

Mama: (In tears) Yewura…

Yewura: (Overcome with emotion) Mama…

Mama: We must let the child go so she can fulfill her destiny, I will die childless, the gods gave and are taking…

Yewura: Yes, we will let her go, a living child is better than a dying one… Mama and Yewura: (To the Village Priest) We let her go …

Village priest: Never a thing disconnected from its creator and purpose of creation ever survived against the will of the gods… For what is man’s purpose on this earth if he does not fulfill the purpose…his purpose?

(With this he hits his staff on the ground and a vulture appears flying in a circle above the child, he hits the ground with his staff again and the vulture falls dead at the foot of the convulsing child and it ceases as quickly as the vulture hit the ground dead).

The Crowd: (Excited murmurings, which turn into praises for the gods).

Village Priest: (To Mama) Weep not woman for according to the time of life you shall be compensated of a child’. (Saying this he holds Akua’s hand, helps her up, and says to her…).

Village priest: Come my priestess, come my priestess, let us together dance the dance of Odomankoma… (they both move a leg in sync as if walking away and freeze).

(Lights fade out slowly).

Scene Ends

my only child. The gods should pick another young maiden from the households of those who have many children….

First Man: (continues) and has not for a moment ceased convulsing…

Yewura: (Overcome with emotion) Mama…

Yewura: Yes, we will let her go, a living child is better than a dying one… Mama and Yewura: (To the Village Priest) We let her go …

Scene Ends
