content.raw_content:
SCENE ONE – DA’S HOUSE

(Drums. A group of about six young men and women rush onstage dancing Gota, a recreational traditional Ghanaian dance. They dance joyfully for a short while.)

(NARRATOR – an old woman, NANA, chewing a stick and using a walking stick – enters slowly from the audience, moving towards the stage. The dancers notice her, quickly sit in a semi-circle facing the audience as the drumming dies down.)

YOUNG DANCERS(excitedly)Nana, tell us a story! Nana, tell us a story!

NARRATOR(Holding up a hand)Hush, hush, children. I will tell a story, yes. That is why I am here.(Beat, leans in)But this story I am going to tell is not for you, it is about you – for our wonderful audience.

YOUNG DANCERS(Deflated)Ohhh…

NARRATORI will compensate you with a story about them on the next moonlit night.(Points gently at the audience)Now, go home to your families. Since this story is not for you, you do not need to be here anyway.

YOUNG DANCERSOkay, Nana…

(They spring up, dance briefly as an exit flourish, then scatter offstage in pairs, laughing and chatting.)

NARRATOR(Calling after them)See you next moonlit night!

YOUNG DANCERS(Off, some shouting back)Okay, Nana!

(She spits out debris from the chewing stick, then turns to the audience.)

NARRATORMy name is Nana, as you have already heard. When you are as old as me, the name that truly fits you is the one that tells your age, or at least gives an idea of it.

(She speaks and spits intermittently as she chews.)

NARRATOR(Holding her waist)Akos!

AKOS(Off)Yes, Nana!

NARRATORA stool, please. Bring me a stool.

(AKOS runs on with a stool.)

NARRATOR(Pointing upstage right)Put it there. I must sit where I can tell the story, be in the story, and yet not block the eyes of our audience.

(AKOS positions the stool upstage right. NANA sits carefully.)

NARRATORYou can go and prepare for your entrance later, my child.

AKOSYes, Nana.

(AKOS exits.)

NARRATOR(To herself, then to audience)Such a bright and agile child…(Shakes her head)Too bad she is in such a dysfunctional family.

(Turns fully to the audience.)My children, listen. Gone are the days when people lived harmoniously in our small village, content with what they had and happy. Happy with family, happy with the little possessions they had, and clever enough to make the most of that little.

Now things are different. In these times you call “modern,” people try to outdo one another. They are never content, and that disease has entered our small town of Wodzenewodze. Just look at this family, for instance…

(DA, a man in his 40s, walks in whistling. He sits on the floor, legs spread, and begins sharpening his cutlass on a small rock.)

DA(To himself)I don’t feel like going to the farm today. In fact, I don’t feel like going any day.(Thinks)When was the last time I even went? Hmm. A long time. And I’m not planning to go today either.

(He drops the cutlass.)

DACalling outAkos! Akos eeeii! Bring me my iPhone 12!

AKOS(Off)Yes, Da!

(AKOS enters with the phone and hands it to him.)

DA(To audience, proudly displaying phone)You see? I have iPhone 12. Very soon, I will get iPhone 13… what’s the name again?(Thinks)Aha! iPhone 13 Pro Max. Just wait and see. When I sell this year’s cocoa harvest, I’ll go and spend some time – and some moneeeeyyy – in the city.

Who says a farmer doesn’t need a vacation? The bank might be on my neck, but even the mouse is bold enough to live in the same house as the cat. All my children will follow my steps and be farmers here too. I will not allow them to waste their youth in a classroom staring at books they can’t even understand, when they can farm instead.

(Pause)What is school? School can wait – if it’s even worth going at all. See, I’m not very educated. I didn’t even go to JHS. But when I speak, you hear me, don’t you?

CHORUS(If used from audience or offstage)Yes, we do.

DAWhen I eat, does it not enter my stomach?

CHORUSYes, it does.

DAWhen I get money, can I not still spend it?

CHORUSYes, you can.

(He bursts into exaggerated “rich man” laughter.)

DAI live a very good life off my farm. The same farm I’ve used as collateral for a bank loan.

Next week, there is a family funeral. My brother and his family will be coming for the first time in five years. I want him to see how well I’m living here.

(Looks at phone)Let me call him.(To phone)Siri, call my brother.

(He waits; no answer.)

DATsk. These city people are villagers paa. They don’t even know how to answer calls.

(Laughs, then calls)Akos! Akossss!

AKOS(Entering)Yes, Da.

DATake this property of mine back safely where you took it from.

(He hands her the phone.)

DAWait. Why is your face like that? You’ve frowned your face like you swallowed bitter leaves.

AKOSNothing, Da o…

DAAbomination! How can you frown your face, darken the clouds and say nothing is wrong? Talk, I’m listening.

AKOS(Quiet but firm)Da, I want to go to school.

DA(Shocked)No! Why should I waste money on school when there are better things to use money for? If you don’t want to farm and carry firewood like every regular girl your age, go back inside. And don’t mention school again.

No school for you or any of your siblings. That money can go to better things – like the iPhone 13 Pro Max I’m saving for.

(Calls out)Children! Children!!!

(The CHILDREN come out, arranged in their tattered clothes, clearly unhappy.)

DALook, I know none of you is happy about the new “developments” in this house… but I’m trying to make you better people in this community.

(They snicker under their breath.)

DAI gave birth to nine of you so you could help me. The farm work is plenty. Now, five of you are this grown and you say you want to go to school? It won’t happen! My farm is small. I alone cannot work hard enough to feed all nine of you. If you help on the farm, we can manage.

CHILDREN(In unison)But Da…

DABut Da what?(Angry)I paid school fees for years, and what happened? You were still sacked because I said I wouldn’t pay again. Is it my fault things are hard? I went to your so-called Headmaster, wearing my kente, and explained that I have to take care of my family too. He got angry. I got angry. I didn’t pay for a term—

CHILDRENThree terms, Da.

DAErh, three terms – and so?

From now, come and help me on the farm. Besides, God blessed me with girls, and I must begin to enjoy the fruit of my labour. I’ll start marrying you off, one after the other.

CHILDRENShockedAh, Da!

DAAh, Da what? Should I not benefit from what my loins have produced? None of you five girls is a child, only Akos. And even she will be ripe in three years.

(Scanning them)Fourteen to nineteen. You are ready for marriage.

(MA enters, excited.)

MA(talking fast)Husband, I saw a beautiful expensive cloth at the market! I can’t wait to buy it and show my friends. And for the funeral, I need a new black and red cloth. I have to send it to the seamstress too—

(Stops, noticing the children)What is going on here?

DAYes, my dear, we must look very expensive at the funeral.(Laughs)I don’t even know why I’m sharpening this cutlass. I’m not going to the farm. I’m waiting for those boys to come and clear that small land for me. They’re charging a lot, but what is money compared to my rest?

AKOS(Quietly, but with courage)But Daddy, all this money you are wasting on funeral clothes and expensive phones could at least send one of us to school. If you say you cannot send all of us, maybe one…

DAWill you keep quiet? For your age, you talk about things bigger than you. I should marry you off first! I don’t want to hear “school” again. My father didn’t go to school, his father didn’t, his father’s father didn’t. What are you talking about?

JAMENA(Softly interjects)But Uncle Timo, your brother went to school.

DA(Sharp)And that is why he only has two children! Is he man enough to handle nine like me? What work do I do? Yet I live an expensive life. Don’t provoke me.

(To MA)Woman, why are you just standing there as your children talk to me like I’m their mate? Have you joined them? You haven’t even given me breakfast!

MANo o.(To the children)My friends, out of our sight! Go and set the firewood for heavy breakfast, just how your father likes it.

(The children murmur and exit to obey.)

NARRATOR(Speaking over the scene)Look at them: husband, wife, and nine children. All they think about is buying and buying and buying.

The father used to be a good farmer, until five years ago when he took a loan to expand his cocoa farm. All the money is wasted on unnecessary things. He has only this year – maybe this very month – to pay, or else the family land, used as collateral, will be taken away.

Lights fade / transition.

SCENE TWO – THE STREET

(NARRATOR steps a little forward.)

NARRATOR(To audience)Pay close attention to these ones coming. A gossip’s tongue can tell you everything happening in a whole household in just five minutes.

(GOSSIP 1, 2, 3 enter, walking as if they’re on their normal rounds.)

GOSSIP 1Did you see Akosua’s mother’s flashy dress at the market yesterday? Eei, that family, they have money o.

GOSSIP 2If they have money, why are eleven people living in one small room, with no window, not even a mosquito net?

GOSSIP 1(Laughs)Eei, my sister, how did you even know there’s no net?

GOSSIP 2I know things.

GOSSIP 1But why are their children not going to school anymore? I hear not even one of them is in school— all of them have been sacked.

GOSSIP 3My sister, say it again o. What work does the man do that he’s always buying new clothes and shoes? And have you heard?

GOSSIP 1 & 2(Leaning in)Heard what?

GOSSIP 3They say he uses an iPhone 12!

GOSSIP 2Eeeeeiii! Once upon a time he was a farmer. Now he’s just a spender!

(They all burst into laughter.)

GOSSIP 3I heard his brother in the city has only two children, but they’re in university and well cared for. Yet if you see him, he doesn’t even look rich.

GOSSIP 1Exactly! Don’t judge a book by its cover. The poor are trying to live rich while the rich live like the poor. Girls!

GOSSIP 3I also hear his daughter Jamena is pregnant.

GOSSIP 1Is that news? It was bound to happen.

GOSSIP 2Are you now hearing? Hmm. Anyway, the “rich man”—(Emphasizing)—the “rich man” whose house is collapsing is throwing a pre-birthday party for himself this evening. His birthday is next week, but he just felt like it. The music is the invitation: if you hear it…

GOSSIP 1 & 3…you attend!

GOSSIP 1Eiii… money is talking.

(They laugh. Music starts – party music. Some youngsters appear, dancing a short Shaku Shaku-style formation.)

(NARRATOR rises from her stool, steps forward.)

NARRATORThere is trouble! The bank is coming, while the cocoa farm is burning.

CHORUS(Off or on)Fire! Fire! Fire! Oh, oh, oh! Your farm is burning, Da! Your farm is burning, Da!

(All on stage panic and rush off in different directions – party cut short. Only NARRATOR remains.)

Lights shift.

SCENE THREE – THE STREET (LATER)

(GOSSIP 1, 2, 3 sneak on, looking around as if trying not to be seen.)

GOSSIP 1Did you see what happened yesterday?

GOSSIP 2Oh yes. When the Spender’s debtor came for him.

GOSSIP 3He had used his farmland and that small house as collateral. He didn’t invest the loan well, and now look.

GOSSIP 2It’s sad. A man living beyond his means, refusing to work, wasting what little he has.

GOSSIP 1He is in biiiiiiig trouble now. His whole family too. They are running up and down, trying to raise money to pay back.

GOSSIP 3They should call the rich uncle in the city. Maybe he can help.

GOSSIP 1 & 2Mmmm…

(They continue miming gossip as NARRATOR steps forward.)

NARRATORYou see, people, when a child insists on touching something red-hot, fire will teach that child a lesson.

The Spender would have been thrown out of his house if not for his brother’s intervention. He might even have ended up in jail for failing to pay his huge debt.

Let us learn to live within our means and be content with what we have. Be frugal, and use the little resources you have wisely. Wise resource management is key. And never deny your children their right to education, because human resource is the ultimate resource.

(Turns, calling)Come here, all of you!

(The whole cast – children, DA, MA, GOSSIPS, YOUNG DANCERS – run back on and gather around her.)

NARRATORI hope you have learnt your lessons through this experience?

CHORUS / ALLYes, we have…

Lights fade.

END OF PLAY

GOSSIP 1Eiii… money is talking.

SCENE THREE – THE STREET (LATER)
(GOSSIP 1, 2, 3 sneak on, looking around as if trying not to be seen.)
GOSSIP 1Did you see what happened yesterday?
GOSSIP 2Oh yes. When the Spender’s debtor came for him.
GOSSIP 3He had used his farmland and that small house as collateral. He didn’t invest the loan well, and now look.
GOSSIP 2It’s sad. A man living beyond his means, refusing to work, wasting what little he has.
GOSSIP 1He is in biiiiiiig trouble now. His whole family too. They are running up and down, trying to raise money to pay back.
GOSSIP 3They should call the rich uncle in the city. Maybe he can help.
GOSSIP 1 & 2Mmmm…
(They continue miming gossip as NARRATOR steps forward.)

(Turns, calling)Come here, all of you!
(The whole cast – children, DA, MA, GOSSIPS, YOUNG DANCERS – run back on and gather around her.)
NARRATORI hope you have learnt your lessons through this experience?
CHORUS / ALLYes, we have…
Lights fade.
END OF PLAY

content.title: Rewrite the Stars (Tonight)
content.subtitle: A stage play in nine scenes
content.raw_content:
A short stage play / dance-theatre piece

CAST OF CHARACTERS

ROSALYN – A young woman, sensitive, romantic, wounded by past relationships.MICHAEL – Roselyn’s former boyfriend, affectionate but emotionally insecure.LINDEN – A sincere man, drawn to Roselyn, but limited by his own fears and boundaries.EARLIER GENTLEMAN – A memory/figure representing a previous love in Roselyn’s life (can be double-cast as MICHAEL if desired).BALLERINA – A dancer who embodies Roselyn’s inner emotional world.

SETTING

Various locations:

A stage in an auditorium (for dance sequences)

A library

A park

Linden’s living room

Time: The present.

Music: “Rewrite the Stars” from The Greatest Showman, used in sections as indicated (licensed or suitable instrumental arrangement).

SCENE 1

The Stage of an Auditorium

(Blackout. A soft golden-yellow spotlight fades up on the BALLERINA center stage. She wears a red dress.)

Music: The first male verse and chorus of “Rewrite the Stars” begins (instrumental or vocal).

(The BALLERINA dances a mimetic solo that suggests longing and reaching out toward an unseen partner. Her movement builds in intensity with the chorus, then softens as the verse ends.)

(As the music transitions out of the chorus, her movements slow. She finishes in a still, vulnerable pose. The spotlight slowly fades to black.)

Blackout.

SCENE 2

Library

(Lights rise on ROSELYN seated alone at a library table with books open in front of her. The space is quiet. A soft, neutral wash.)

ROSELYN sits staring at the books but not reading.

(Beat.)

EARLIER GENTLEMAN enters, carrying a small stack of books.

EARLIER GENTLEMAN(Softly, friendly)Need a hand?

(He takes some of her books and places them on the table. They share a brief smile.)

(Short montage can be suggested through lighting shifts and minimal movement, or done as stylized action.)

(He sits beside her, occasionally glancing at her with a warm smile.)

(He places a small gift box on the table and slides it toward her.)

(He gently takes her hands in his, holding them for a moment.)

(Beat.)

Suddenly, EARLIER GENTLEMAN is gone. The light shifts back; ROSELYN is alone at the table.

ROSELYN looks around, confused.

(Beat – confusion turns to realization.)

She lowers her head as tears fill her eyes. She takes a tissue, wipes her tears, closes her books carefully, and gathers her things.

(She stands, pauses for a moment as if listening for his presence, then exits, still dabbing her eyes.)

Lights fade.

SCENE 3

Park

(Lights up on a simple park setting: a bench, suggestion of trees. ROSELYN and MICHAEL enter, holding hands, laughing softly.)

(Brief physical sequence to show their connection: they walk, playfully bump shoulders, share a private joke.)

(Beat.)

(Images/moments can be indicated by stylized action or projections.)

MICHAEL kneels to tie ROSELYN’s loose shoelace.

He gently brushes a strand of hair from her face.

He holds her hands against his chest with both of his.

He embraces her in a warm hug.

They sit on the bench.

MICHAEL(Still a bit breathless from laughing)You know, I could do this every day.

ROSELYN(Smiling)Walk in circles and make bad jokes?

MICHAEL(Grinning)Exactly that.

(Beat. His smile fades slightly as he grows more serious.)

MICHAELRosy, I need to tell you something.

ROSELYN(Still light, trusting)Okay, love. What is it?

MICHAEL(Taking a breath, subdued)I… I don’t think I can do this anymore.

ROSELYN(Frowning)Do what?

MICHAELThis.

ROSELYN(Leans in)What is “this,” Michael?

MICHAEL(Beat, then blurts)This relationship.

(Silence.)

ROSELYN(Standing, stepping away from the bench)What are you talking about? Why?

MICHAEL(Stands slowly)I’m sorry, Roselyn. I’m scared. I don’t think I’m ready for this kind of love.(Beat.)I don’t want to keep pretending and hurt you even more later.

ROSELYN(Voice trembling)But you’re already hurting me now.

(He reaches toward her face to wipe a tear. She pulls away quickly.)

ROSELYNDon’t.

(Beat.)

MICHAEL looks at her one last time, then turns and walks away, not looking back.

ROSELYN watches him go, then her knees give a little and she sinks back onto the bench.

She begins to cry, trying to stifle the sobs but failing.

(After a moment, she pulls a book out of her bag, opens it, and reveals a photo of herself and MICHAEL. She takes the photo out, folds it into quarters with shaking hands, and places it carefully in the corner of the bench.)

(Beat.)

She wipes her face with a tissue, stands, and exits slowly, leaving the folded photo behind.

Lights fade.

SCENE 4

Linden’s Living Room

(Lights rise on a modest living room. ROSELYN sits on a sofa, arms loosely wrapped around herself. LINDEN kneels in front of her, holding a small jewelry box.)

LINDENRoselyn, please… just listen to me.

ROSELYN(Shaking her head, eyes turned away)Linden, I can’t go through this again.

LINDENI’m not asking you to jump into anything.(Beat.)Just let me be here. Let me care about you.

(He opens the jewelry box, revealing a delicate piece of jewelry, and offers it.)

ROSELYN(Looks at it, then pushes it gently back toward him)I can’t accept that. Not now. Maybe not ever.

(She starts to rise. LINDEN reaches out and lightly holds her wrist—not forceful, but desperate.)

LINDEN(Softly)Don’t run from me too.

(Beat. She looks away.)

Lights begin to fade as the moment stretches, then transition.

SCENE 5

The Stage of an Auditorium – Dance

(Spotlight up on BALLERINA, again in the red dress. The rest of the stage is dark.)

Music: Female verse of “Rewrite the Stars” beginning with “You think it’s easy…”

(BALLERINA’s movement now shows resistance and inner conflict: reaching out and pulling back, circling an invisible partner, collapsing inward and then forcing herself upright.)

(At the end of the verse, she turns away from the invisible partner, wrapping her arms around herself. The light fades.)

Blackout.

SCENE 6

Linden’s Living Room

(Lights up on the same living room. ROSELYN sits on the sofa, LINDEN now on a chair nearby, leaning slightly forward.)

LINDENI love you, Roselyn.(Beat.)I’m not like the others who stepped in and out of your life. I love you, and I will keep loving you if you let me.(Leans in)Let me love you tonight… and tomorrow… and the day after that.

(Beat.)

ROSELYN(Softly, eyes fixed on her hands)I don’t know if I can believe that.(Beat.)My heart’s been broken so many times it feels beyond repair. Love always seems to end in rejection and loneliness. I’ve learned to suffer in silence.

(She looks up, meeting his gaze.)

ROSELYNThis thing… this thing called love never seems to last. They all said to me, “Let me love you tonight.”(Beat.)But like a candle in the wind, the flame always went out.

LINDENThis time can be different.(Leans forward more)This love can last. Just give me a chance, Roselyn. Let me love you genuinely, starting tonight.

(Beat. ROSELYN holds his gaze for a long moment, then a shy smile trembles onto her lips. She looks away, torn.)

Lights dim slowly, transitioning to the next scene.

SCENE 7

The Stage of an Auditorium – Duet Section

(Spotlight on BALLERINA. The stage remains otherwise dark.)

Music: Duet section of “Rewrite the Stars.”

(BALLERINA dances as though with an unseen partner: turns, near-lifts, almost-embraces. Her choreography mixes hope with hesitation. She reaches for something that almost—but never quite—settles into place.)

(At the end of the duet, she spins away and freezes in a fragile, open pose, as if waiting to see if someone will catch her.)

Lights fade.

SCENE 8

Linden’s Living Room / Various Locations (Montage)

(A flexible staging: the montage can be suggested via lighting changes and minimal set pieces.)

(Lights: warm afternoon – ROSELYN and LINDEN share ice cream, laughing; a drip of ice cream falls, they laugh harder.)

(Lights shift to evening – they walk under streetlights, close together.)

(Lights shift to night – they sit side by side on a rooftop or balcony, fingers intertwined, looking at the stars.)

(Lights shift to early morning – they share a simple breakfast. ROSELYN looks genuinely relaxed and happy.)

(The montage ends with a clear look at ROSELYN’s renewed trust.)

Lights settle back into LINDEN’s living room.

ROSELYN(Jumps up joyfully)Linden, let’s go see my parents.(Beat, excited)I want them to meet you.

(LINDEN’s smile fades just slightly. He hesitates.)

LINDEN(Shakes his head slowly)Roselyn… I don’t think that’s a good idea.

ROSELYN(Playful at first, lightly tugging his hand)Come on, don’t be shy. They’re going to love you.

(She pulls him toward the open door. She steps through the doorway. He stops at the threshold.)

(Beat.)

ROSELYN turns back. LINDEN remains in the doorway, unmoving.

ROSELYN(Confusion shifting into fear)Linden…?

LINDEN(Quietly, almost apologetic)I didn’t lie to you.(Beat.)I did love you. I still do. But I never promised more than tonight, did I?

(Silence.)

ROSELYN stands outside, suddenly alone in the light. LINDEN stays framed in the doorway, a clear line between them.

(Beat.)

The light around LINDEN slowly fades until only ROSELYN is lit.

ROSELYN’s shoulders sink. She turns away from the doorway and walks off, slowly, the joy drained from her steps.

Lights fade to black.

SCENE 9

The Stage of an Auditorium – Final Dance

(A single spotlight rises slowly on the BALLERINA center stage. Her movements are slower now, weighted with sorrow.)

Music: Final female verse and closing lines of “Rewrite the Stars.”

(She dances with smaller, more contained gestures—reaching toward the audience, then toward the empty space where a partner should stand, but nobody appears. Each reach falls back into herself.)

(As the music reaches its emotional peak, she begins a controlled, slow fall to the floor, one arm reaching up as if trying to hold onto a fading light.)

(She settles on the ground, the last note lingering. She mouths—or softly whispers—the word:)

BALLERINA(Almost inaudible)Tonight.

(The spotlight tightens to a small circle around her face or outstretched hand, then fades to black.)

End of Play.

content.title: Taraji Says No to Plastic!
content.subtitle: An environmental novella for brave young minds across Ghana and beyond
content.raw_content:
### PROLOGUE – ON THE SAHARA



### The Sahara was wide and golden. The sand shimmered like tiny stars.In the middle of that great desert, Mama Africa walked slowly, carrying a carved wooden stool.


Her dress shone with all the colors of the continent. When she sat down, the wind grew quiet. One by one, her children – the Sub‑Saharan countries – came and sat around her in a big semi-circle. Each brought a stool, each wore their own bright colors.

Mama Africa closed her eyes. She could feel something heavy on her heart. Far away, in a town called Cape Coast in Ghana, gutters were choked with plastic. Streets, schools, rivers, even beaches were covered with sachets, bottles, and bags.

“My children,” she said, her voice cool like water to a thirsty throat, “something that once looked like a blessing has become a big problem. Plastic is filling our land and our seas. But I will not just complain. Today, I will send help.”

She lifted her hand towards the West.

“I send three spirits,” she said, “to visit a brave child. I see a girl in Cape Coast. Her name is Taraji – it means Hope. She will help wake up her people.”


### The desert wind carried her words away, towards the sea.



### CHAPTER 1 – SATURDAY IN CAPE COAST


In Cape Coast, the morning woke up with noise and smell and color.

Birds chirped on mango trees. A rooster crowed again and again, as if shouting, “Get up, get up! Today is important!”

In a small compound house, Mama Tara stirred a pot of steaming porridge. Elder Kwesi, her husband, chased chickens in the yard, laughing as they dodged him.

Then they heard it: “Ko ko ko! Keke keke ke! Ko ko ko!”


### The gong-beater’s metal gong rang across the town.


“The people of Cape Coast, I greet you!” the gong-beater shouted. “When the bat flies in the morning, the birds must pay attention! Our king, Osabarima Kwame Nti I, calls everyone – old and young, strong and weak, wise and simple – to his palace next Saturday before the cock crows thrice in the afternoon.”

He struck the gong again: “Ko ko ko!”

“You must not come empty-handed,” he went on. “Come with the coconut of Solomon. In the palace we shall break it and find a solution to the plastic that is swallowing our town!”

“Ko ko ko ko!”

Inside the yard, Elder Kwesi finally caught a chicken and lifted it up.

“Mama Tara,” he called, smiling, “today I want chicken soup with fufu. Please, kill this one.”

Mama Tara took the chicken gently. “My husband,” she said, “the king wants ideas about plastic. What do you think is the solution?”

Elder Kwesi wiped sweat from his forehead. “We clean together every two weeks,” he said. “But the rubbish returns. It multiplies. The problem begins where the rubbish is born. If we want a solution, we must change how we use and throw away things.”

“You are right, my wise husband,” she replied. “That is why you are an Elder. What can beat the wisdom of a man?”

Elder Kwesi laughed softly. “The wisdom of a woman, my wife. The wisdom of a woman.”

Behind the door, a girl was listening. Her name was Taraji. Her eyes were sharp and curious.

“I’m going to find my own idea,” she whispered to herself. “I don’t want my town to drown in plastic.”


### CHAPTER 2 – TARAJI AT SCHOOL


On Monday, Taraji reached school early, as usual.

a pile of fresh green leaves

### CHAPTER 4 – THE NIGHT OF THREE VISITORS

“We also need rules,” she added. “Maybe the town can have ‘No Plastic Days’ in the market. Maybe we can have ‘Clean-Up Clubs’ in schools, led by children. We can teach each other.”

“My king,” she said, “I had a dream. I saw our land clean again. I saw people using baskets, leaves, and reusable bottles. I saw children leading the way. Please, let us start today. Together, let us say no to plastic!”

“Today,” he said, “we have learned that wisdom also lives in the head of the girl-child. We will follow these ideas.”

Teach our people to use cloth bags and baskets instead of plastic bags.

Work with groups to recycle plastic into useful things.

Create children’s Clean-Up Clubs. The children will help lead.”

She raised her hands.

Mama Africa smiled. “Good children,” she said. “Good children.”

Hope had begun.

“Here, plastic is not thrown away,” the Spirit said. “It is turned into something useful.”
They passed a small garden. Bottles were cut and used as plant pots. A woman watered tomatoes growing in them.
“That’s a nice idea!” Taraji said. “We can do that at school.”
Next, they visited a market. Some shoppers held cloth bags. A woman carried a basket on her head. A boy filled his reusable water bottle at a clean water station.

“Many people are choosing to use less plastic,” the Spirit explained. “They say ‘No, thank you’ to plastic bags. They use reusable bottles and cups. They go back to baskets and leaves and other natural things.”
Taraji imagined herself telling her friends, “Let’s all bring our own water bottles. Let’s all bring cloth bags to the market.”
The Spirit smiled. “You see? A few small changes, made by many people, can heal those brown patches on my robe.”
Taraji looked at the robe again. The green had spread.
“I want my town to look like this,” she said softly. “I want to help.”
“That is why we came,” the Spirit said. “You have a voice. Use it.”
He touched her forehead with one finger.
“Remember these three words,” he whispered. “Reduce. Reuse. Recycle.”
Taraji whispered them back. “Reduce. Reuse. Recycle.”
Everything faded. At last, she slept peacefully until morning.
CHAPTER 5 – PREPARING FOR THE PALACE
The next day in class, Madam Ismailia clapped her hands.
“Scientists!” she called. “Share your ideas! What can children do about plastic?”
Hands rose everywhere.
“We can have two bins in each class,” Adeaze suggested. “One for plastic, one for other rubbish.”
“We can make a ‘No Littering’ club,” said Thabo. “If we see rubbish on the ground, we pick it up and put it in the right bin.”
“We can carry our own water bottles and stop buying sachet water every day,” another student added.
Then it was Taraji’s turn. She stood up, heart beating fast.

“Madam,” she said, “I think we need to change what we use, not just where we throw it. We can ask food sellers to use leaves instead of plastic when possible. We can bring our own containers from home. We can use baskets and cloth bags instead of plastic bags. And we can make things from used bottles, like flower pots or even benches.”
Her classmates murmured. These ideas were big, but they felt possible.
Madam Ismailia clapped. “These are excellent ideas,” she said. “You must share them at the king’s meeting. Remember, children also belong in the circle of wisdom.”
Taraji smiled shyly. Inside, she remembered the Spirit’s words: You have a voice. Use it.
CHAPTER 6 – THE KING LISTENS
The following Saturday, the palace courtyard was full.
Women in cloth wrappers. Men in smocks. Children in their best clothes. Everyone fanned themselves under the hot sun, waiting.
At the front sat King Osabarima Kwame Nti I on his stool, shining in gold ornaments. Beside him were his elders, including Elder Kwesi and Elder Akosua.
The gong-beater struck his gong three times. “Ko ko ko!”
“My people,” the king said, “we are here because plastic is choking our town. We clean, yet the rubbish returns. Today, we will listen to ideas – from anyone who has a wise heart.”
Silence filled the air.
The elders shifted. No one spoke.
Taraji’s hand squeezed her mother’s.
“Mama,” she whispered, “can I speak?”
Mama Tara looked into her daughter’s eyes. They were bright with courage.
“Why not?” she said softly. “You should go. Wisdom also lies in the head of the girl-child.”
Taraji’s older brother leaned in. “Mother, no,” he whispered. “She is just a child. And a girl. Will anyone listen?”
Mama Tara straightened her back. “They will listen,” she replied. “Because truth does not choose only the heads of men.”
She nudged Taraji gently. “Go.”
Taraji stood. Her legs felt wobbly, but she remembered turtles in plastic and goats in pain. She walked to the center of the courtyard.
“My king,” she began, voice trembling, “please allow me to speak.”
Before the king could answer, Elder Osei frowned.
“Child,” he said sharply, “this is a meeting for great minds. Stand aside. You are just a girl.”
The crowd murmured. Some nodded. Others shook their heads.
Elder Akosua’s eyes flashed. She stood up.
“What is this, Elder Osei?” she said. “Am I not a woman, yet I sit here as an elder like you? Is my mind smaller because I am a woman?”
The courtyard fell silent.
The king’s voice rang out, strong and clear. “Elder Osei,” he said, “you will apologize to Elder Akosua and all the women and girls of this kingdom. Wisdom does not live in one gender.”
Elder Osei bowed his head. “I am sorry,” he said.
The king turned to Taraji. “My wise girl-child,” he said, “speak. We are listening.”
Taraji took a deep breath. Her fear faded a little.

“Thank you, my king,” she said. “I am Taraji. I am in primary school. I love my town. But every day, I see plastic everywhere – in school, in the gutters, on the beach. We learned in science class that plastic causes floods and sickness and kills animals. I don’t want Cape Coast to drown in rubbish.”
She paused and looked around. Many faces were watching, curious.
“I am only a child,” she continued, “but I know we can do three things: reduce, reuse, and recycle.”
She lifted one finger.

“First – reduce. We must use less plastic. We can bring our own cloth bags when we go to the market. We can say ‘No, thank you’ when someone offers us a plastic bag for just one small thing. Food sellers can use leaves and paper more, not plastic packs every time.”
She lifted a second finger.

“Second – reuse. Before we throw plastic away, we can ask, ‘Can this become something else?’ We can use bottles as flower pots in our yards. We can collect strong plastic and work with carpenters to make benches for schools. We can refill bottles instead of buying new ones every day.”
She lifted a third finger.

“Third – recycle. We must separate our rubbish. One bin for plastic, one for other waste. The plastic can be collected and taken to a place where it is turned into new things. Our schools and churches can teach us how.”
She looked up at the elders.
“We also need rules,” she added. “Maybe the town can have ‘No Plastic Days’ in the market. Maybe we can have ‘Clean-Up Clubs’ in schools, led by children. We can teach each other.”
Taraji’s voice grew stronger.

“My king,” she said, “I had a dream. I saw our land clean again. I saw people using baskets, leaves, and reusable bottles. I saw children leading the way. Please, let us start today. Together, let us say no to plastic!”
For a moment, everything was still.
Then Elder Kwesi jumped to his feet and clapped. Mama Tara clapped too, tears in her eyes. Elder Akosua stood and clapped. Children began to chant, “No to plastic! No to plastic!”
Soon the whole courtyard was roaring with applause.
The king lifted his hand for silence.
“Today,” he said, “we have learned that wisdom also lives in the head of the girl-child. We will follow these ideas.”
He looked at the elders. “From now on,” he declared, “we will:
Put separate bins for plastic and other waste in our town and schools.
Teach our people to use cloth bags and baskets instead of plastic bags.
Work with groups to recycle plastic into useful things.
Create children’s Clean-Up Clubs. The children will help lead.”
He turned back to Taraji. “Taraji,” he said, “you have given us hope. You are truly your name.”
CHAPTER 7 – A NEW CHANT
On Monday, Taraji took her project work to school. On the front page she had written in big, bold letters:
“TOGETHER, LET US SAY NO TO PLASTIC!”
Her drawing showed children holding cloth bags, using leaf wraps, putting rubbish into different bins, and standing proudly beside a clean river.
Madam Ismailia pinned Taraji’s project on the notice board.
At assembly, the headteacher spoke.
“From today,” he said, “our school will have a ‘Green Club’. Taraji will be one of the leaders. We will separate our rubbish and use less plastic.”
The students cheered.
Later that week, at the Sahara, Mama Africa sat again on her stool. Around her, the Sub‑Saharan countries listened.
“Children in Cape Coast have spoken,” she announced. “They say, ‘Together, let us say no to plastic.’”
She raised her hands.
The countries replied as one, “Yes, we will!”
Mama Africa smiled. “Good children,” she said. “Good children.”
And far away, in a little house in Cape Coast, Taraji smiled in her sleep.
Hope had begun.
THE END

people.full_bio:
Born in Ghana with a Bachelor of Fine Art Degree in Theatre from the University of Ghana, Linda Emefa Daniels is a dramatist, poet, and storyteller awarded the prestigious 2021/2022 Sophia Lokko Memorial Prize for Best Graduating Student in Theatre Arts.

"If a nation loses its storytellers, it loses its childhood." — Peter Handke

Linda writes from lived experiences, keen observation, Christian faith, cultural heritage, and the quiet and loud conversations of life. Her prose and verse delve into the human condition with unapologetic vulnerability and hope.
